Whole shares and residual cash: A portfolio is a collection of holdings and cash. Asset allocation describes how its value is divided among asset types or holdings. A stock represents ownership in a company; a bond is a debt investment in which an issuer owes payments under its terms. An exchange-traded fund (ETF) holds a basket of assets and trades on an exchange; its diversification depends on what it holds.

Diversification means spreading exposure across different holdings, sectors or asset types instead of depending on one source of returns. It can reduce the impact of a single company's poor performance. It does not remove market-wide risk or guarantee a profit, and correlated holdings can still decline together.
Published closes and benchmarks: A benchmark is a reference used to compare performance. A market index tracks a defined group of securities under stated rules and can serve as a benchmark. Comparing a portfolio with a relevant benchmark helps describe relative performance; beating it over one period does not prove investing skill or predict future returns.

Return measures the change in value relative to starting value, after accounting for the costs and cash flows included in the calculation. Compounding means later returns apply to a value that already includes earlier gains or losses. A percentage gain after a percentage loss is applied to the reduced value, so equal percentage changes need not cancel out.
